pages.text:
*Days without rain: 119. Buckets from the spring: 7.*

"Start small," Mei said. Her voice was quiet, but it did not shake. She looked at Yun, who was still trembling near the edge of the dry lakebed.

"The smallest thunder is a sneeze," said Tao. He held up one finger, then two, then all five, as if counting the syllables.

"Thunder is a sudden expansion of air," said Hua. She adjusted her ponytail, the yellow ribbon fluttering against her red jacket. "If you want the science."

Yun blinked his amber eyes. He shifted his weight, his pale gold belly brushing the cracked mud. "I would rather not, thank you," he said, in that careful, polite way he had. "But I am willing to try."

The three children leaned in, forming a tight circle of yellow boots, red jackets, and braids around the dragon. The mountain seemed to hold its breath. Yun drew in a long, shuddering breath, and the mist around him curled tighter, like a scarf pulled up against the cold.

A tiny hiccup escaped him.

It was soft and round, sounding exactly like a wooden drawer sliding shut in an empty room.

Tao clapped his hands. "There it is! That was loud!"

pages.text:
Mei straightened her back, and her shoulders settled. "Breathe with me," she said. "In for four. Hold for one. Out for four."

Yun’s whiskers puffed out, stiffening in the thin air. He followed her count, his nose twitching with every number. On the first try, nothing happened, only a faint whistle of wind moving through his antlers.

"Again," Mei said.

On the second try, he held the breath a little longer. When he released it, a low rumble rolled out of his chest. It was not a boom, nor a crack, but soft and deep, no louder than a cat purring on a warm roof tile.

Tao cheered so loudly that the sound bounced off the rocks, and Yun leaped two feet into the air, his claws scrabbling at the empty space above him.

"I apologize to the sky!" he yelped, landing with a soft thud. "I did not mean to startle the atmosphere!"

Hua was grinning. "That was actually quite steady," she admitted.

pages.text:
Hua stepped closer, tilting her head. "You are clenching your throat," she said. "That is why it gets stuck. Look."

She stood beside the dragon, her shoulder almost touching his whiskers. She relaxed her jaw, letting her face soften completely. "Like this. No tension. Just air."

Yun tried to copy her. He stared at his own reflection in a small, clear pool of water near the shore. He mimicked Hua’s face, then his own. Both ended up with their jaws hanging open, slack and round.

Tao laughed until he fell backward off a flat rock, landing in a cloud of dry dust. He scrambled up, wiping grit from his green tiger shirt. "You look like two surprised fish!"

The little valley of Black Pool rang with their laughter. It was a bright, sharp sound that had not visited this spot in a hundred years. Yun looked at the children, and for the first time, the mist around him did not look like a hiding place.

pages.text:
They practiced for the rest of the afternoon. The sun moved across the sky, painting the rocks in shades of gold and long, purple shadow. They started with a purr, then a low growl, and finally a proper small rumble that rolled once around the rocks and came back to them, echoing off the stone walls.

Yun looked astonished. His amber eyes were wide, and he did it again. A little wind stirred the mist, lifting it in slow, lazy swirls while the surface of the almost-dry pool rippled, just slightly, as if something heavy had passed over it.

"Can you do a big one?" Tao begged, bouncing on his heels until his yellow boots squeaked. "Just a little bit bigger than that."

Yun went stiff, his shoulders hunching as the rumble died in his chest, trapped and heavy. He shook his head in a slow, careful motion. "No," he said softly. "Not yet. I am not ready for that size."

The silence that followed settled over them, heavy and still, waiting for someone to break it first.

pages.text:
The dragon hid his head under a wing of mist that he did not have. It was a clumsy, awkward gesture, and it only made him look more like a shy child than a creature of the sky.

"There," he said. His voice was barely a whisper. "You see? It is not that I cannot. It is that I will not. I see their faces every time. The screaming. The running. I cannot do that again."

Mei did not argue. She did not offer the science, or the luck of the boots, or the logic of the list. She simply sat down on the cold stone beside him. She placed her hand on the rough rock, right next to his claw. She breathed in for four, held for one, and breathed out for four.

She stayed there, steady and quiet, while the mist swirled around them both.
